entities.name: Baba Ishak
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Baba Ishak was a charismatic dervish and heterodox religious leader who ignited the Babaî Rebellion, a major messianic uprising that convulsed the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in Anatolia from 1239 to 1241. Operating from the marginalized fringes of Seljuk society, Ishak successfully mobilized thousands of disenchanted Turkmen nomads and impoverished peasants, promising a new era of justice and challenging the centralizing authority and orthodox Islamic establishment of Sultan Gıyaseddin Keyhüsrev II. His movement, rooted in a blend of Sufi mysticism and indigenous Anatolian beliefs, transcended mere political grievance to become a profound social and religious challenge to the existing order.

The rebellion, erupting in the spring of 1240, rapidly spread across central and eastern Anatolia, from Elbistan to Amaseia. Baba Ishak, proclaiming himself a prophet or even a divine manifestation, commanded a devoted following that overwhelmed initial Seljuk resistance. His dervishes and Turkmen warriors captured key cities like Kayseri and Sivas, inflicting significant defeats upon the Seljuk army, including the annihilation of a force led by the Seljuk vizier. The sheer speed and scale of the insurgency underscored the deep-seated popular discontent and the fragility of Seljuk control over its peripheral territories.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Baba Ishak's 1240 rebellion critically destabilized the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, directly contributing to its decisive defeat by the Mongols at the Battle of Köse Dağ in 1243 and profoundly reshaping the political future of Anatolia.
